children: By Alicia McElhaney, Jodi Xu Klein and Alexander Gladstone
Florida's high-speed railroad Brightline is planning an imminent chapter 11 bankruptcy filing in New Jersey, according to people familiar with the matter.
The Fortress Investment Group-backed company plans to cut its debt to roughly $2.7 billion as part of the restructuring, down from about $5.5 billion, said the people.
A group of municipal bondholders and lenders, including Assured Guaranty, BlackRock, First Eagle, Invesco, Nomura and Nuveen, agreed to provide $490 million in exit financing, they said.

Brightline's operating company will remain outside chapter 11 to keep the train line operational while the company restructures its capital structure through its holding company in bankruptcy, the people said. Brightline is expected to finalize and potentially distribute a restructuring support agreement as soon as Thursday.
The company's $2.2 billion in senior secured debt will remain outstanding in the reorganized Brightline, the people said.
The nation's largest private intercity rail operator has struggled with tepid ridership growth that failed to produce the revenue needed to service its heavy debt burden.
In April, the railroad issued a going-concern warning, cautioning that it lacked the liquidity to sustain it as a viable business and raising the possibility of bankruptcy.

The warning triggered a jockeying for control among senior municipal bondholders, bond insurers and junior debtholders offering competing financing that could either stave off a bankruptcy filing or fund the proceeding.
Brightline also faces personal-injury lawsuits tied to fatal accidents on its track, though it hasn't been held liable.
